Iran: Tehran calls US response on Hormuz "unconvincing", but Qatar keeps talks going

On Wednesday, November 4, Iran said Washington's response to its plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz did not meet its seven conditions. Donald Trump confirmed strikes on an Iranian island, another oil tanker was attacked, and Qatar says both sides remain at the table [1][2][5].

According to Al Jazeera, Iran called the US response to its plan "unconvincing" on November 4. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, said it did not meet Tehran's seven conditions, including the lifting of sanctions and an end to the US naval blockade [1].

The Iranian plan provides for reopening the strait within two days, provided the United States meets these seven demands. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says the outcome depends on the answers given to Iran's questions [3][5].
Donald Trump confirmed he ordered strikes on an Iranian island near the strait, and another oil tanker was attacked in the area, according to Al Jazeera [1].
The spokesperson for Qatar's foreign ministry says both parties "remain engaged in the negotiation process" and that Qatar is facilitating a "real-time exchange of proposals" [2][5].

The Iranian delegation, led by Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi, passed messages to the Americans via Qatar for three days in Doha, then left the city. An official said it was "not because of difficulties", that a draft agreement was circulating and that another meeting remained possible [3][4].

On the US side, Donald Trump says the war will end "very soon, one way or another". Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the president has not decided to launch new strikes and would prefer a diplomatic solution [1][2].
In markets, US oil (WTI) lost about 8% on Wednesday, a drop that Yahoo Finance links mainly to the outcome of the US elections [6].

Key takeaway: the two sides are not talking about the same thing. Iran ties the reopening of the strait to seven conditions, including the lifting of sanctions and an end to the naval blockade; it considers the US response insufficient, but nobody is leaving the table [1][5].

Qatar is acting as a mailbox. The Iranian delegation did not negotiate face to face: it passed on messages that Doha relays in real time. That explains why you hear both "no, this is not enough" and "the talks are continuing" [3][5].

For the economy, the strait is the sensitive point: part of the world's oil passes through it, and a single attacked tanker is enough to push prices up. US crude fell 8% on Wednesday, but that decline reflects a political hope, not a signed agreement [1][6].

Caution: these are statements by the parties, reported by media outlets, and each side presents the situation to its advantage. No independent source yet confirms the exact content of the draft agreement [2][3].

If you fill up your car or heat your home with diesel or gas, this issue affects your prices: a deal would push oil down, a new incident would push it up. Nothing is settled, so don't count on a lasting drop at the pump tomorrow.

Eurozone: inflation climbs to 4% in October, its highest in three years, and the ECB moves closer to a rate hike in December

According to Eurostat's first estimate published on November 4, eurozone inflation rose from 3.8% to 4.0% in October, a three-year high. Energy is the driver (+20.8% over one year), while inflation excluding energy and food stays at 2.5% [1][2].
Eurostat estimates annual eurozone inflation at 4.0% in October, up from 3.8% in September. That is double the European Central Bank (ECB)'s 2% target and a three-year high, according to CNBC [1][2].
Energy prices rose 20.8% over one year, compared with 18.9% in September: they explain most of the increase [1][2].
"Core" inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was stable at 2.5%. Services accelerated from 3.2% to 3.3% [1][2].
Gaps between countries are wide: Lithuania has the highest rate (6.1%), Malta the lowest (2.3%) [2].
The ECB left its rates unchanged at its October meeting. Before the release, markets were giving a little over 72% odds of a hike in December, according to Seeking Alpha [1][3].
Joachim Nagel, president of the Bundesbank, is keeping the door open to a hike in December, according to an account of his remarks [4].
This is a flash estimate: the final October figures will be published on November 18 and its components may be revised [2][3].

Key takeaway: this inflation comes mainly from energy, not from an overheating economy. When oil, gas and electricity cost 20.8% more than a year ago, the increase shows up immediately at the pump and on bills [1][2].

For the ECB, the dilemma is real. Raising rates makes credit more expensive and slows activity, but does not lower the price of oil. The fact that core inflation stays at 2.5% could, according to one commentator, indicate that the cycle of increases is nearing its end; services at 3.3%, on the other hand, show that the increase is starting to spread to other prices [1][3].
The gap between Lithuania (6.1%) and Malta (2.3%) is a reminder that a single policy rate applies to twenty very different economies, which complicates the ECB's task [2].
Caution: the December decision will also depend on the November figures and on how oil evolves. Market probabilities shift from one week to the next [3][4].

If you have a variable-rate mortgage, an ECB rate hike would show up in your monthly payments; with a fixed rate, nothing changes for you. Energy prices, for their part, are already weighing on your budget.

Ukraine: Russian strike on a school used as a shelter kills at least 33, and Zelensky comes to Berlin to ask for energy and money

On Monday, November 2, Russian bombs hit a school in the Zaporizhzhia region that served as a shelter and aid distribution point: at least 33 dead according to Volodymyr Zelensky, who mentions up to 70 victims. On November 3 in Berlin, he made the case for his power grid and the €11.6 billion in German aid planned for 2027 [1][2][3][6].

The strike took place on Monday, November 2 in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region. According to Zelensky: "The Russians struck first as people were arriving, a few aerial bombs. Then a second blow, with more bombs, this time on the shelter" [1][4].

The school served as a shelter and, every Monday, as a humanitarian aid distribution site. The Kyiv Independent first counted 24 dead, including two rescuers and four police officers; the toll then rose to at least 33 dead according to Zelensky [1][2].
CBS News reports that the toll has risen to 40 dead, and that Zelensky mentioned a toll that could reach 70 people while calling for air defenses [3].
The Russian Defense Ministry says it targeted Ukrainian forces in the area and claims up to 25 Ukrainian soldiers killed; Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians [1].

According to Zelensky, the strike came just before a new salvo of hundreds of drones and dozens of cruise and ballistic missiles against energy infrastructure, despite Donald Trump's calls for an energy truce [5].

On Tuesday, November 3 in Berlin, he met the president of the Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, on protecting the power grid: "the situation of our grid is very difficult right now, with major outages in many regions" [6][7].
Germany has included €11.6 billion in aid to Ukraine in its draft 2027 federal budget, not yet voted on; Zelensky thanked Berlin and asked that this decision be adopted [6][7].

Key takeaway: the war is hitting civilians and the economy at the same time. A shelter bombed twice, then power plants and power lines targeted: Ukraine must protect its people and its grid as winter approaches [1][6].

If Zelensky is insisting on energy, it is because outages are already severe, as he said in Berlin. The German money for 2027 does not solve the winter of 2026, but it guarantees the duration of support, which matters for the Ukrainian state's budgets [6][7].

Two versions clash: Kyiv speaks of civilians killed in a shelter, Moscow of a strike against military personnel. The toll is not final and has varied from one outlet to another (24, 33, 40, up to 70 mentioned): we therefore report the figures attributed to Zelensky, as such [1][3].
On the political front, Zelensky said he hopes the outcome of the US elections will help Ukraine, notably through Congressional support, in an interview with German television ZDF [8].

If you live in Europe, this war also goes through your budget: aid to Ukraine weighs on German and European public finances, and therefore on debt and taxes. Nothing is settled for 2027 until the Bundestag has voted.

US-China: trade truce runs until January 10, but November 10 remains a key date for rare earths

Announced in late September during Xi Jinping's state visit to Washington, the two-month extension of the trade truce pushes the pause on certain tariff increases back to January 10, 2027. Several deadlines nonetheless fall on November 10, including China's suspension of rare earth controls [1][2][3].

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced, as Xi Jinping began his state visit, that the truce, which was due to expire in November, was extended until January 10. Depending on the sources, the announcement dates from September 23 or 24 [1][3].

China had suspended for one year, until November 10, 2026, its export controls on rare earths decided on October 9, 2025, its Ministry of Commerce confirmed. This suspension holds only as long as the truce holds [2][3].
China's April 2025 controls, which target seven specific rare earths, were never suspended and still require a license from the Ministry of Commerce [2].

On the US side, Washington suspended its so-called "Affiliates Rule": a law firm noted that the Bureau of Industry and Security had not yet published the notice formalizing the two-month extension [4].
178 "Section 301" exclusions (US tariffs on Chinese products) also expire on November 10, 2026 [5][6].
Licenses remain a sticking point: Reuters reported that some US companies waited more than six months to obtain one [2][3].
Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected in Shenzhen for the APEC summit on November 18 [6].

Key takeaway: November 10 is no longer the end of the truce, but it is not an insignificant date. What China put on pause, the October 2025 controls on rare earths, takes effect again on that date if nothing is renewed [2][3].
Rare earths are metals used in magnets, from electric car motors to defense equipment. A license that is delayed means a factory that waits: the stakes lie as much in delays as in bans [2][3].
The extension is short, two months. Analysts describe it as a tactical truce rather than a fundamental change, according to Coface [7].
As of this Thursday, we found no announcement on renewing China's November 10 suspension: this is the point to watch in the coming days [6].

If you work in automotive, electronics or renewable energy, these metals matter for costs and lead times. For consumers, the effect shows up later, in the price and availability of certain devices and electric vehicles.

Wall Street surges 3% the day after the midterms, and oil falls 8%

On Wednesday, November 4, the Dow Jones gained 3.03% to 53,356 points, its best session since April 2025, after the Democrats' victory in the midterm elections. The S&P 500 rose 1.58% and the Nasdaq 1.44%, while US oil lost about 8% [1][2][3].
The Dow Jones rose 1,569.40 points (3.03%) to 53,356.12; the S&P 500 rose 1.58% to 7,688.62; the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.44% to 25,736.51, according to CNBC [1].
It is the Dow's best session since April 2025 [1].
Investors read the clear-cut election result as the end of political uncertainty; Donald Trump's acceptance of the result was part of the picture, according to The Washington Times [4].
Energy stocks fell the most, with US WTI crude shedding about 8% during the session [2][3].

A market recap also notes that US government bonds rose, on the idea that a divided government would limit spending, and that the dollar index fell to 101.21 at one point, its lowest since September 30 [5].
Other recaps show very different figures (Dow down 0.4%). We use CNBC's closing figures, consistent with the scale of the rise described by Yahoo Finance and TheStreet [1][2][3].

Key takeaway: a stock market hates uncertainty. When an election result is clear, investors know where they stand and take on risk again; the 3% rise comes far more from that than from any specific economic measure [1][4].

The drop in oil is the most striking point. According to the recaps, it is linked to the hope that a divided Congress will reduce tensions in the Middle East. Yet the same day, Iran called the US response unconvincing: the market reacted to a hope, not to a fact [2][5].
History is rather reassuring, without guaranteeing anything: since 1950, the S&P 500 was higher twelve months after each of the 19 midterm elections, but the sample is small [6].

If your savings are invested in stocks (PEA, unit-linked life insurance, index funds), a +3% session changes nothing over a horizon of several years, any more than a -3% session would. We are not saying to buy or sell.

How it works: why an election result moves the stock market

A stock's price reflects what investors expect from future earnings, adjusted for risk. Before an election, nobody knows which laws, taxes or tariffs will follow: investors demand a higher risk premium, and therefore pay less for stocks. When the result comes in, part of that uncertainty disappears at once and prices rise, even if nothing concrete has changed yet. Some sectors also depend on specific decisions (energy, health, defense) and react according to what the new balance of power suggests. Oil, for its part, also moves with geopolitics: if conflict risks seem to recede, the risk premium on a barrel shrinks [1][2][5].
Midterm elections and the stock market: what history has shown
Since 1950
The S&P 500 was higher twelve months after each of the 19 midterm elections, with an average gain of 15.1% [6].
Uncertainty weighs before the vote and fades afterward; but the sample is small and nothing guarantees that it will happen again [6].
According to a Motley Fool analysis, these are the only two midterm elections followed by a negative twelve-month return [7].
The pattern is not a law: there are exceptions, even in a very favorable sample [7].
Since 1938
According to Fidelity, the S&P 500 recorded a price increase in the twelve months following these elections in 95% of cases [8].
Elections have rarely been the main driver of long-term returns, according to Fidelity [8].

On Wednesday, November 4, an ounce of gold gained nearly 3% to about $4,054, climbing back above $4,000 after a fixing price of $3,913 on Friday. Silver jumped 4.6% to $52.49. The Democratic victories weakened the dollar [1][2][3].
Spot gold traded at about $4,053.68 an ounce, up $116.29 (2.95%) on the day. Fortune noted $4,046 at 8:45 a.m. New York time [1][2].

The articles link the rise to the Democrats' victory in Congress and to a weaker dollar: the dollar index fell to 101.21 at one point, its lowest since September 30 [1][3][4].
Key takeaway: gold pays no interest and is priced in dollars. When the dollar falls, it becomes cheaper for buyers paying in other currencies, which supports demand [1][3].
The rebound does not change the overall picture: gold remains well below its January record, about $5,595 an ounce on January 29, 2026 [5][6]. Just last Friday, it hit its lowest in a year [9].

What follows will depend on US rates: a Fed hike in December would make gold, which pays nothing, less attractive compared with investments that pay interest, and that is the argument analysts put forward on Friday [7].

Physical gold (coins, bars) and gold funds follow these movements. For a French saver, the metal is not a guarantee of stability: its price moved 3% in one session this week, and fell by more than 3% on Friday. We are not saying to buy or sell.

How it works: why gold reacts to the dollar and to interest rates

Gold is sold in dollars on global markets. If the dollar falls, a European or Asian buyer pays less in their own currency, and demand can increase. In addition, gold pays neither interest nor dividends: when rates rise, bonds and interest-bearing accounts pay more, and gold becomes less attractive; when rates fall or the dollar weakens, the opposite happens. Finally, gold is a safe haven, but not always: in the event of a sharp fall in stock markets, some investors sell it to raise cash elsewhere, which explains last week's abrupt drops [1][3][7].

news.2026-11-05-bresil-copom-selic-pause: Brazil: central bank pauses rate cuts at 13.75% after Lula's reelection

On Wednesday, November 4, the monetary policy committee (Copom) unanimously left the Selic rate at 13.75%, ending five cuts in a row. Reuters links the pause to the prospect of higher inflation after the reelection of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva [1][2].
The Copom, chaired by Gabriel Galípolo, voted unanimously to keep the Selic rate at 13.75%, after five consecutive cuts [1][3].
The decision was expected: 33 of the 48 economists polled by Reuters and 26 of 31 in a Bloomberg survey forecast a pause [1][2].
Before the meeting, inflation stood at 4.58% and the real was weaker; the rate remains about 9 points above inflation [3].
Officials raised their inflation forecast for 2027 to 4.7%, from 3.9% [2], and repeated that monetary policy must remain "substantially restrictive" [1].

Key takeaway: a central bank cuts rates when it considers prices under control. Here, it is stopping because the 2027 inflation forecast is rising, and because Lula's reelection, according to Reuters, raises fears of more public spending [1][2].
The Copom gave no signal about what comes next; its next meeting, on December 8 and 9, is the last of the year [3].

In Brazil, a high policy rate makes loans and purchases on credit more expensive; for a foreign investor, it makes investments in reais more rewarding but the currency more sensitive to political news.
